title: Team Members Who Are Always Late
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece takes a firm stance on chronic lateness as a leadership and culture issue, not a minor personality quirk. It argues that tolerating one team member's habitual tardiness silently punishes everyone who does show up on time, sending an implicit message that team rules apply unevenly and eroding both trust and the leader's own credibility. Interestingly, it notes that chronically late people are often among the most optimistic team members, whose can-do attitude leads them to underestimate how long things take. The essay's resolution frames lateness as binary: either the person doesn't value the work, or they do but the team can't rely on them -- and good leaders confront that directly, with no exceptions for star performers.
points: Tolerating chronic lateness from one team member implicitly punishes everyone who makes the effort to be on time.
Accommodating lateness sends a symbolic message that team rules and courtesy don't apply equally to everyone, eroding trust and the leader's credibility.
Chronically late team members are often the most optimistic people on the team, whose can-do attitude leads them to misjudge how long tasks take.
Lateness reflects one of two problems: the person doesn't value the work, or they do but the team can't depend on them.
Good leaders hold everyone to the same standards on this issue, with no exceptions even for top performers.
quotes: Once this pattern takes hold, it can be very hard to break and can be highly consequential not only for the team member, but also for the leader's credibility.
Leaders who accept or tolerate a team member's chronic lateness unintentionally punish those who are on time.
This small acceptance has huge implications for team trust and cohesiveness and quickly erodes the leader's credibility.
Complicating matters even more, chronically tardy team members are often the most optimistic people on the team.
Either the team member believes what the team is doing is not important to them, or they believe it is important to them but fully acknowledge the team can't depend or count on them.
Good leaders hold everyone to the same standards and rules. No exceptions, even for star players.
